opus-5.5.text:
I think Marc Raibert's contribution is foundational, and honestly it's hard to overstate. Back in the 1980s, when most people in robotics were thinking about walking as a slow, statically stable process — keep the center of mass over the support polygon, move one leg at a time — Raibert went in almost the opposite direction. At the MIT Leg Lab, and before that at CMU, he built hopping machines: one-legged hoppers, then bipeds and quadrupeds, that were fundamentally dynamic. They were always falling and catching themselves.

What I find most beautiful about his work is the simplicity of the control decomposition. He split the problem into three nearly independent parts: control the hopping height through thrust, control forward speed through where you place the foot, and control body attitude through hip torque during stance. That's an incredibly elegant insight. It showed that you don't need a perfect model of the whole system to get robust, agile behavior. You need the right abstraction. A lot of what came later, like the spring-loaded inverted pendulum line of thinking and capture-point ideas, carries some of that spirit.

Then of course there's Boston Dynamics. He took that research lineage and pushed it toward real machines — BigDog, Atlas, Spot. For a long time, those videos were what the whole world thought of when they pictured a legged robot. They set the bar for what "agile" meant, and I think they inspired a whole generation of researchers, including many of us who later worked on learning-based approaches.

Now, from where I sit today, the field has shifted quite a lot. Reinforcement learning in simulation, sim-to-real transfer, large-scale training — these have made locomotion much more accessible, and a lot of the hand-designed controllers are being replaced. But I don't see that as diminishing Raibert's contribution. In a way, he answered the existence question first: he proved that dynamic legged locomotion is physically achievable and controllable on real hardware. And he emphasized building real machines, testing them, and letting physics teach you. That attitude — respecting hardware, respecting dynamics — is still something I think every robotics researcher should carry with them.

So for me, he's both a scientific pioneer and a kind of cultural figure for the field. He made legged robots feel real, and that changed what people believed was possible.

fable-5.1.text:
Marc Raibert is, to me, the father of dynamic legged locomotion. Before him, most people doing legged robots were thinking in terms of static stability, keeping the center of mass inside the support polygon, moving slowly and carefully. Raibert went the other direction. In the early eighties at Carnegie Mellon and then at the MIT Leg Lab, he built a one-legged hopping machine, which sounds almost absurd, but it was a brilliant choice. A one-legged hopper can't be statically stable at all. It has to balance by moving. So he forced the problem down to its essence: how do you control a system that is constantly falling and catching itself?

What came out of that was his three-part controller, hopping height, forward speed, and body attitude, decoupled and handled almost independently. It is remarkably simple, and it still works. If you look at a lot of modern quadruped controllers, even the learned ones, you can see the lineage. The foot placement heuristics, the idea of a spring-loaded inverted pendulum as the model for running, those ideas trace back to his lab.

The second thing I'd emphasize is that he insisted on building real hardware and making it work in the physical world. He wasn't satisfied with a simulation. That culture carried into Boston Dynamics. BigDog in the mid-2000s, then Atlas, then Spot, each one was a demonstration that dynamic balance could survive contact with reality, getting kicked, slipping on ice, walking on rubble. A lot of us in the field grew up watching those videos and deciding this was what we wanted to do.

And the third contribution, maybe underrated, is patience. Boston Dynamics spent decades on this before it became commercially viable. Raibert was willing to be a research company for a very long time. Now, with the AI Institute, he is again putting money into basic questions about athletic intelligence rather than chasing the next product. So I would say his contribution isn't only the technical ideas, as important as they are. It is that he established a way of doing legged robotics, dynamic first, hardware first, and long horizon, that defined the field.

astra-6.text:
I think Marc Raibert’s central contribution was to show that balance in legged robots is a dynamic process. You don’t have to keep the robot statically stable at every instant. You can let it fall, in a sense, and use the next foot placement to recover—much as we do when we run.

His work on hopping robots made that idea concrete. It showed how relatively simple control principles could produce surprisingly robust movement. Through his research and later Boston Dynamics, he helped turn legged locomotion from a theoretical possibility into something people could see working in the physical world.

To me, that’s his lasting influence: he changed both how researchers approached the problem and what they believed was possible.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Marc Raibert’s contribution is foundational. He helped establish that a legged robot doesn’t have to remain statically balanced at every instant. It can use motion—hopping, running, and continually adjusting its footing—to stay upright. That made dynamic balance a practical engineering approach.

His early work also showed how a difficult control problem could be broken into manageable parts, such as controlling hopping height, forward speed, and body posture. Through Boston Dynamics, he helped bring those ideas into machines that made the possibilities of legged robotics tangible to a much wider audience.

To me, his greatest contribution is that combination of physical intuition and experimentation: building a machine, watching what happens, and using that experience to understand locomotion more deeply.
